item.title: Buy-to-let costs soar twice as fast as rental income
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Buy-to-let landlords are facing mounting financial pressures as rising costs outpace rental income growth, according to recent analysis of HMRC data. Lettings platform Hello Neighbour found that expenses now consume nearly 60p of every £1 earned in rent, up from 47.8% just five years ago. This trend highlights the growing challenges for property investors in the private rental sector.

Rising Costs Outstrip Rental Income

Over the past five years, buy-to-let expenses have surged by 56%, while rental income has increased by just 26%. In the 2024-25 financial year, landlords declared £34.75bn in allowable expenses against £58.99bn in rental income. This marks a significant shift from 2019-20, when expenses totalled £22.33bn against income of £46.69bn. The average landlord now faces £13,700 in expenses, compared to £20,500 in rental income.

Finance costs have emerged as the largest expense, accounting for 37% of total outgoings. Around 1.15 million landlords claimed residential finance costs averaging £11,148 each. Repairs and maintenance also represent a substantial portion of expenses, with 1.92 million landlords spending an average of £3,339 annually. These figures exclude capital improvements such as kitchen upgrades or energy efficiency measures.

Future Challenges for Landlords

Looking ahead, buy-to-let landlords face additional financial pressures. Privately rented homes in England must meet an EPC rating of C or higher by October 2030, unless exempt. Additionally, the reformed Decent Homes Standard is set to apply to the sector from 2035, potentially requiring further investment in property upgrades.

Mortgaged landlords are also grappling with the impact of Section 24, introduced in April 2020. This legislation prevents individual landlords from deducting residential finance costs when calculating taxable rental profits. Instead, they receive a basic-rate tax reduction worth 20% of these costs. Companies, however, remain unaffected by this restriction and can still deduct finance costs in full.

Phil Shelley, Chair of Hello Neighbour, noted: “A sector housing a fifth of the country cannot absorb costs rising at twice the rate of income indefinitely. Landlords are being asked to fund upgrades the country wants through increasingly squeezed margins.”

With costs continuing to rise faster than rental income, landlords may wish to carefully assess their financial position and consider strategies to manage expenses effectively in this challenging market.

item.title: July figures offer fresh warning for the housing market
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent HMRC data has revealed a slight dip in UK residential property transactions during July, raising fresh concerns about the housing market's resilience amidst ongoing economic uncertainty. Whilst seasonal adjustments show a 2% monthly decline, the broader picture remains more positive with year-to-date figures maintaining healthy growth compared to 2022 levels.

Mixed signals in transaction data

The provisional figures present two different perspectives on market activity. Seasonally adjusted completions fell to 96,710 in July – down from June's 98,390 and 1% below the same period last year. However, the non-adjusted data tells a more encouraging story, showing a 3% monthly increase to 106,620 transactions, representing a 5% annual uplift.

When examining the wider April-July period, the market appears stronger still. Some 389,490 non-seasonally adjusted residential transactions were recorded – a 15% increase compared to the same timeframe in 2022. Experts caution that these figures remain provisional and should be viewed as lagging indicators, typically reflecting sales agreed two to four months earlier.

Structural challenges persist

Industry voices have highlighted how the modest July dip underscores deeper systemic issues in the property market. Maria Harris of the Open Property Data Association noted: "The housing market remains vulnerable to uncertainty, but we must also address the structural problems making home moves unnecessarily difficult."

Key concerns include:

  • A fragmented and slow-moving transaction process
  • High rates of failed transactions due to inefficiencies
  • Lack of standardised property data sharing between parties

The government's proposed reforms to modernise homebuying could help address these challenges, though experts stress the importance of implementing robust data standards and secure information-sharing systems to make transactions more reliable.

Market caution continues

Mortgage professionals report that many potential movers remain hesitant, with Paul Adams of Pepper Money observing: "The brief improvement we saw in June hasn't developed into sustained growth." This aligns with broker feedback suggesting homeowners are:

  • Staying put to retain favourable mortgage rates secured in previous years
  • Adopting a wait-and-see approach amid economic uncertainty
  • Considering home improvements rather than moving in some cases

Whilst the housing market continues to demonstrate resilience compared to 2022's figures, these latest statistics serve as a reminder that underlying challenges persist. Both policymakers and industry participants may need to focus on modernising transaction processes to create a more efficient and reliable system for all involved.

item.title: Landlord Law Blog roundup for August
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Landlord Law Blog has released its August roundup, offering valuable insights for landlords and tenants alike. The month’s highlights included updates on tenant rights, landlord responsibilities, and practical guidance for navigating the UK’s rental market. Whether you’re a property owner or renting a home, these resources could prove useful in staying informed about the latest legal developments.

Key Updates for Tenants

One of the standout updates for August was the relaunch of the Renters’ Guide, which has been refreshed to reflect changes brought about by the Renters’ Rights Act. This comprehensive resource aims to help tenants understand their rights and responsibilities, covering topics such as tenancy agreements, deposit protection, and eviction procedures. With the rental market evolving, this guide could be a helpful tool for those looking to stay informed about their legal protections.

Guidance for Landlords

For landlords, the blog continued to provide practical advice on managing rental properties effectively. August’s posts included tips on complying with legal requirements, handling tenant disputes, and maintaining properties to meet safety standards. With regulations becoming increasingly complex, landlords might find these insights particularly valuable in ensuring they remain compliant while managing their portfolios.

Staying Ahead in the Rental Market

Both landlords and tenants face unique challenges in today’s rental market. The Landlord Law Blog’s August roundup emphasised the importance of staying updated on legal changes and understanding how they impact rental agreements. For tenants, this means being aware of their rights, whilst landlords may wish to focus on meeting their obligations to avoid potential disputes or penalties.

As the rental landscape continues to evolve, resources like the Landlord Law Blog could play a crucial role in helping both parties navigate these changes. Whether you’re a tenant seeking clarity on your rights or a landlord looking to stay compliant, these updates offer a useful starting point.

item.title: Property industry reacts to latest Nationwide house price data
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK housing market showed little movement in August, with house prices rising by just 0.2%, according to the latest data from Nationwide. Annual house price growth remained steady at 1.6%, reflecting a market that continues to tread cautiously amidst ongoing economic uncertainty. Factors such as fluctuating interest rate expectations and rising energy costs have contributed to this subdued activity, though Nationwide suggests that the impact of energy prices on broader inflation may be limited.

Affordability Gradually Improves Amidst Challenges

Despite the sluggish market, Nationwide’s Chief Economist, Robert Gardner, noted that affordability is slowly improving. House price growth continues to lag behind earnings growth, which could benefit prospective buyers. However, higher mortgage rates have partially offset these gains, leaving many homeowners and potential buyers weighing their options. Gardner expressed optimism that market activity could regain momentum in the coming months, particularly if energy price pressures ease and confidence returns to the market.

Gardner also highlighted that private sector wage growth has shown signs of easing, potentially giving the Bank of England more flexibility in its monetary policy decisions. This could play a crucial role in determining whether further interest rate hikes are necessary to bring inflation back to target levels.

National Park Properties Command Premium Prices

In addition to its monthly house price analysis, Nationwide conducted research into the impact of location on property values, specifically focusing on homes within National Parks. The findings revealed that properties located in these areas attract a significant premium, averaging 24% higher than comparable homes elsewhere. In monetary terms, this equates to an additional £66,500 for a typical property.

Gardner explained that National Parks are highly sought-after due to their scenic landscapes and access to outdoor activities. Strict development controls, which limit new housing construction, also contribute to the higher prices. For homeowners considering a move to these areas, this premium reflects the unique appeal and limited availability of properties in such locations.

As the UK housing market navigates a period of uncertainty, these insights from Nationwide provide a clearer picture of current trends and potential opportunities for buyers and sellers alike.

item.title: New shadow housing secretary appointed after James Cleverly steps down
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Katie Lam MP has been named as the Conservative Party's new Shadow Housing, Communities and Local Government Secretary following Sir James Cleverly's resignation from the role. The change comes as Cleverly, MP for Braintree, prepares to seek his party's nomination for the 2028 London mayoral election. His departure from the shadow housing brief after just over a year in post creates an opportunity for fresh scrutiny of government housing policies under new leadership.

New Shadow Housing Secretary takes the reins

As the newly appointed shadow housing minister, Lam assumes responsibility for holding the government to account on key property market issues including housebuilding targets, planning system reforms and housing affordability. The Weald of Kent MP will also oversee local government and communities policy within her expanded brief. The Conservative Party emphasised Lam's dual focus on boosting housing supply while protecting local community interests in their announcement.

Lam steps into the role during a period of significant challenges for the housing sector, with ongoing debates about planning permission reforms and concerns about meeting annual housing construction targets. Industry commentators will be watching closely to see how the new shadow secretary approaches these longstanding issues that directly impact mortgage holders and prospective buyers.

Political context of the appointment

The shadow cabinet reshuffle occurs against the backdrop of Cleverly's mayoral ambitions, though he hasn't yet confirmed whether he'll resign as an MP. The Conservatives haven't selected their London mayoral candidate, leaving Cleverly's political future temporarily uncertain as he prepares his campaign. Meanwhile, Lam's promotion signals the opposition party's intention to strengthen its housing policy platform ahead of the next general election.

Housing professionals suggest Lam's background as a backbench MP with constituency experience dealing with local planning matters could prove valuable in scrutinising government housing strategies. Her appointment comes at a time when both major political parties are under pressure to address the UK's chronic housing shortage and make homeownership more accessible.

The property industry will be particularly interested to see whether Lam maintains Cleverly's policy direction or implements new approaches to housing supply and planning reforms. With affordability remaining a critical concern for borrowers and first-time buyers, political focus on these issues is likely to intensify in the coming months.

item.title: Frozen tax thresholds blamed for property market drag
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK property market is facing a slowdown, with frozen Stamp Duty thresholds and rising house prices creating significant barriers for buyers. Recent data from HMRC reveals a dip in residential property transactions, highlighting the challenges homeowners face in the current climate. Experts suggest that these factors, combined with broader economic pressures, are contributing to subdued activity across the housing market.

Rising Costs and Frozen Thresholds

House price growth, whilst slowing in some areas, continues to push more buyers into higher Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) brackets. The thresholds for SDLT have remained unchanged since 2014, meaning that as property values rise, more homeowners are liable for higher upfront costs when moving. This growing tax burden is becoming a notable obstacle for those looking to purchase a new home.

Mark Cunningham, a partner at Blick Rothenberg, an audit and advisory firm, explains: "Rising property values and frozen SDLT thresholds have resulted in a larger tax burden on most transactions, increasing the overall cost of moving." This is particularly challenging at a time when household budgets are already under pressure from higher borrowing costs and the wider cost of living crisis.

Impact on Market Activity

HMRC’s latest figures show that residential property transactions fell to 96,710 in July on a seasonally adjusted basis, down 2% from June and 1% compared to the same period last year. Whilst activity remains above the levels seen in parts of 2023 and early 2024, the market has yet to establish a sustained upward trend. Cunningham notes that SDLT is not the sole reason for subdued transaction levels, but it is a significant factor influencing buyer behaviour.

"As a transaction tax, SDLT increases the upfront cost of moving and is therefore likely to influence decisions, particularly when household finances are stretched," he adds. This raises questions about whether the government should consider adjusting SDLT thresholds to stimulate market activity.

The Need for Government Action

With housing remaining a key policy priority, there is a strong case for encouraging transactions alongside increasing supply. Cunningham argues: "The property market does not just need homes to be built. It also needs people to move. If transaction levels remain relatively flat despite a more settled economic backdrop, attention should turn to barriers preventing transactions from taking place."

As the government looks to address housing challenges, revising Stamp Duty thresholds could be one way to ease the financial burden on buyers and support a more dynamic property market.

For now, homeowners may wish to carefully consider the costs involved in moving, including SDLT, and explore options to mitigate these expenses. As the market continues to evolve, staying informed about potential changes to property taxes could prove invaluable for those planning their next move.

item.title: New initiative ‘is going to help transform homebuying’
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A new government-backed digital identity trust mark has launched this week, promising to streamline the often tedious process of identity verification during property transactions. The UK CertifID scheme allows approved Digital Verification Service (DVS) providers to display a trusted certification mark, potentially reducing the need for homebuyers to repeatedly prove their identity to different parties involved in their purchase.

How the trust mark could transform homebuying

Currently, property buyers typically need to verify their identity separately with estate agents, mortgage brokers, lenders and conveyancers – a repetitive process that can cause delays. The new scheme aims to create a reusable digital identity that moves with the transaction, allowing different professionals to rely on a single verified check.

Chris Williams of Novus Strategy commented: "After years of waiting, we're now on the cusp of only having to verify identity once. This could allow simultaneous progress on credit checks, underwriting and property searches – potentially reducing the current high rates of failed transactions."

Industry experts suggest the trust mark could particularly benefit:

  • First-time buyers navigating complex processes
  • Those remortgaging or moving home
  • Professionals handling high volumes of transactions

Security and adoption expectations

While participation remains optional for verification providers, market observers anticipate near-universal adoption across the property and lending sectors. The Office for Digital Identities and Attributes (OfDIA) oversees the scheme, which requires providers to meet stringent security standards.

"UK CertifID shows consumers which providers meet all necessary security requirements," Williams explained. "It also gives conveyancers confidence that earlier checks by brokers or agents were fully compliant and can be reused – this is Smart Data in action."

The system represents an example of Horizontal Digital Integration (HDI), where verified identity becomes a reusable component that travels securely with the transaction. As the scheme rolls out, homeowners may find:

  • Reduced paperwork and admin
  • Faster transaction timelines
  • Greater confidence in the security of their data

While the full impact remains to be seen, this initiative could mark a significant step towards modernising the UK's property transaction process – potentially benefiting all parties involved in home purchases and mortgage applications.

item.title: NRLA warns of risk of unqualified agents
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

With rental regulations becoming increasingly complex, the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) has raised concerns about unqualified letting agents operating without mandatory training standards. As more landlords turn to agents to navigate the evolving legal landscape, industry bodies are calling for swifter government action to implement minimum competency requirements.

The growing reliance on letting agents

Recent research suggests a significant proportion of private landlords now depend on letting agents to manage their properties and ensure compliance with housing legislation. The private rental sector has seen over 170 pieces of legislation introduced in the past decade alone, covering everything from tenant fees to safety standards.

Whilst professional agents can provide valuable expertise, the NRLA warns that the current lack of mandatory qualifications means landlords might inadvertently engage unqualified practitioners. This could potentially lead to:

  • Regulatory non-compliance and associated penalties
  • Poor tenant referencing and vetting processes
  • Inadequate property maintenance standards

Calls for industry-wide standards

The NRLA has joined other property organisations in urging the government to accelerate plans for a mandatory qualification framework. Currently, unlike estate agents who must register with a redress scheme, letting agents in England face no minimum training requirements - though Wales and Scotland have already introduced their own accreditation systems.

Industry proposals suggest that a national competency framework could include:

  • Standardised training on housing law and regulations
  • Continuous professional development requirements
  • Clear pathways for agent certification

Landlords using letting agents might wish to verify their current qualifications through recognised schemes such as Propertymark or the NRLA's own training programmes whilst awaiting potential regulatory changes.

As the government continues its review of the private rental sector, the debate around professional standards highlights the growing complexity of property management. With landlords facing increasing responsibilities, the call for properly qualified agents looks set to remain a key industry issue in the coming months.

item.title: Poor maintenance can wipe £59k off property investment
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Landlords who defer essential property maintenance could see their investments lose substantial value, with new analysis suggesting London properties are most vulnerable to depreciation from neglected upkeep. Research indicates rental homes in poor condition may experience price reductions up to £59,000 compared to well-maintained equivalents in the capital.

How maintenance impacts property values

Property experts highlight that maintenance issues tend to compound over time, with small unresolved problems potentially leading to more extensive and expensive damage. Common concerns like damp patches, leaky pipes or cracked tiles might seem minor initially but could develop into structural issues affecting a property's marketability and valuation.

The disparity between maintained and unmaintained properties appears most pronounced in high-value areas, particularly London where property prices remain substantially higher than the national average. However, regional markets across the UK all show measurable value differences between properties in good versus poor condition.

Preventative maintenance strategies

Property owners might consider implementing regular inspections to identify issues before they escalate. A proactive approach could include:

  • Scheduling annual professional surveys to assess the building's condition
  • Setting aside a maintenance budget equivalent to 1-2% of the property's value annually
  • Addressing tenant repair requests promptly to prevent minor issues worsening
  • Keeping records of all maintenance work for future buyers or lenders

While maintenance costs represent an ongoing expense for landlords, the alternative of deferred repairs often proves far more costly in the long term through both diminished property values and potential loss of rental income during major remedial works.

For those considering property investment, factoring in realistic maintenance costs from the outset could help avoid unpleasant financial surprises. Mortgage lenders may also look favourably on well-maintained properties when assessing loan applications, as they typically represent lower-risk collateral.

item.title: Are micro-markets the new reality of property investment?
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Property investors are increasingly focusing on hyper-local market trends, with some postcodes delivering dramatically different performance to surrounding areas. This shift towards 'micro-markets' reflects a growing recognition that city-wide averages often mask significant variations in rental demand, capital growth and regeneration potential.

Why micro-markets matter for property investors

Whilst regional property statistics provide a broad overview, they can obscure lucrative opportunities at a street-by-street level. Savvy investors are now analysing data at granular levels, considering factors such as:

  • School catchment area boundaries creating premium-priced pockets
  • Regeneration schemes transforming specific neighbourhoods
  • Transport links creating sudden demand spikes near new stations
  • Local employment hubs driving rental demand in particular postcodes

This approach reveals how two properties just streets apart might experience completely different market conditions. For example, an area benefiting from infrastructure investment could see prices surge whilst nearby postcodes stagnate.

Identifying promising micro-markets

Property investors might consider several strategies to pinpoint high-potential micro-markets:

  • Tracking planning applications for upcoming developments
  • Monitoring local authority investment in infrastructure
  • Analysing rental yield variations within boroughs
  • Observing tenant demographics shifting in specific areas

Regeneration zones often create particularly interesting micro-markets, where early investors can benefit from price growth before wider recognition. Areas undergoing transport improvements, such as Crossrail in London or HS2-connected regions, have shown how localised property booms can develop.

However, micro-market investing requires thorough due diligence. What appears as an emerging hotspot might be a temporary trend, and over-concentration in one small area could increase risk if local conditions change.

As property investment becomes more sophisticated, understanding micro-markets could help investors identify undervalued opportunities and potentially enhance returns. Whilst not replacing broader market analysis, this hyper-local approach provides an additional layer of insight for building a resilient portfolio.

item.title: Investors missing older renter opportunity
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Property investors may be overlooking a significant market opportunity as the UK's ageing population drives increasing demand for rental homes suited to older tenants. With millions of Britons now renting in their later years, landlords who adapt their properties could find themselves well-positioned to meet this growing need.

The rise of older renters

Recent demographic shifts have seen more people renting properties into retirement age, whether by choice or necessity. Factors such as rising house prices, pension changes and relationship breakdowns have contributed to this trend. Research suggests the proportion of households headed by someone aged 65+ in private rentals has grown substantially in the past decade.

This presents landlords with an emerging market segment that often values stability and longer tenancies. Older renters typically demonstrate reliable payment histories and may be less likely to frequently move home compared to younger tenants. However, this demographic also has specific housing needs that property investors would do well to consider.

Adapting properties for older tenants

While not all older renters require specialist accommodation, simple modifications could make properties more appealing to this growing market. Thoughtful adaptations might include:

  • Walk-in showers instead of baths
  • Grab rails in bathrooms
  • Improved lighting throughout the property
  • Single-level living spaces where possible
  • Non-slip flooring options

Many of these changes represent relatively low-cost investments that could significantly enhance a property's appeal to older tenants. Landlords might also consider properties near local amenities, healthcare facilities and public transport links, which often rank highly on older renters' priority lists.

Market potential for landlords

With demand for suitable rental properties outstripping supply in many areas, landlords who cater to older tenants could benefit from reduced void periods and potentially more stable rental income. Local authorities and housing associations may also be interested in partnering with private landlords to help meet demand for appropriate accommodation.

For property investors looking to diversify their portfolios, the older renter market offers an opportunity to tap into a demographic that's often underserved by the current rental market. As Britain's population continues to age, this trend seems likely to grow rather than diminish in coming years.

Landlords considering this market segment might wish to research local demand and consult letting agents about the specific needs of older tenants in their area. While not without its considerations, the older renter market could represent a stable and potentially profitable niche for the forward-thinking property investor.

item.title: Condition Rating 3: What a Survey Is Really Telling You When It Flags the Windows⧉
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

When reviewing a homebuyer's survey for a period property, many purchasers encounter an all-too-familiar scenario regarding windows. The report typically highlights timber decay issues with a Condition Rating 3 classification – the most severe rating – alongside vague recommendations to consult specialists. While this might appear routine, such findings often conceal significant renovation costs that could impact both the property's value and the buyer's budget.

Understanding Condition Rating 3 for Windows

Under the RICS Home Survey Standard, Condition Rating 3 indicates defects that are serious and/or require urgent repair. For windows in older properties, this typically means:

  • Significant timber decay compromising structural integrity
  • Failed putty or seals leading to draughts and damp penetration
  • Irreparable damage requiring complete replacement rather than refurbishment

Surveyors often phrase these observations cautiously, stating that "specialist advice should be sought" without quantifying potential costs. This measured language reflects their professional indemnity requirements rather than the actual severity of the issue.

Why Window Issues Demand Attention

Period property windows flagged with Condition Rating 3 often represent one of the most substantial hidden costs in older homes. Homeowners may wish to consider:

  • The true cost implications – full sash window replacements in a Victorian terrace can exceed £1,000 per window
  • Energy efficiency impacts – deteriorated windows account for disproportionate heat loss
  • Listed building considerations – replacements often require like-for-like materials and planning consent

Mortgage lenders frequently note these issues in their valuations too. Some may retain funds until repairs are completed, while others might adjust their lending offer based on anticipated refurbishment costs.

While survey language might seem vague, Condition Rating 3 for windows consistently signals necessary – and often expensive – work. Savvy buyers typically request quotes from specialist joiners before committing to a purchase, using this information to renegotiate the price or request repairs from the vendor.

item.title: Opinion: This isn’t a storm agents can wait out – it’s the new climate
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The lettings market has undergone fundamental changes following the introduction of the Renters Reform Act (RRA), with many agents finding their traditional business models no longer deliver sustainable growth. Industry experts suggest that simply weathering the storm isn't enough – letting agencies must actively rebuild using three strategic pillars to thrive in this new landscape.

Strategic Acquisitions: Rebuilding Property Stock

With many agents experiencing dwindling instruction pipelines, strategic acquisitions have emerged as a key solution. Purchasing another agency's portfolio isn't just a fallback option – it represents the most effective method to quickly rebuild managed stock in a stagnant market. However, successful acquisitions require meticulous preparation. Agents might consider establishing robust systems in advance and developing clear 90-day transition plans before completing any deal. Industry data suggests that acquisitions frequently falter when proper integration strategies aren't implemented from day one.

Proactive Lead Generation Strategies

The days of passive lead generation are over in today's lettings market. Landlords continue to require professional services, but many have become more selective about which agents they trust. Rather than waiting for enquiries, forward-thinking agencies are demonstrating their value by clearly articulating the benefits of professional management in the current regulatory climate. Compliance expertise has become a particular differentiator, with agents who proactively explain and implement RRA requirements gaining market share from less prepared competitors.

Diversifying Service Offerings

The RRA's increased compliance requirements present an opportunity for agents to develop new revenue streams. Many landlords now need specialist support that simply wasn't necessary two years ago. Rather than bundling these services for free, innovative agencies are creating properly structured, chargeable offerings. This shift requires moving beyond traditional fully-managed or let-only models to develop tailored solutions that address landlords' evolving needs. Those who successfully monetise these new services often find they improve client retention while boosting profitability.

The lettings sector's transformation demands more than temporary adjustments. By focusing on these three core areas – strategic acquisitions, active lead generation, and service diversification – agents can position themselves for long-term success in the post-RRA market. The most successful operators aren't waiting for conditions to improve; they're actively reshaping their businesses to meet the industry's new realities.

item.title: Landlord hit with £8,000 rent repayment after tenant takes action
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

A landlord in Muswell Hill has been ordered to repay nearly £8,000 in rent to a former tenant after a tribunal ruled the property was an unlicensed house in multiple occupation (HMO). The First-tier Tribunal mandated the refund alongside £341 in tribunal fees following an investigation by Haringey Council into the property's conditions.

Property hazards and licensing failures

The tribunal heard how the tenant endured severe living conditions between May 2023 and May 2024, including extensive mould growth, blocked kitchen facilities, exposed pipework and a collapsed ceiling. Fire safety concerns were also raised, with reports suggesting the property lacked basic precautions such as fire doors and smoke alarms.

Investigations revealed the Leaside Avenue property housed three unrelated tenants, meeting the legal definition of an HMO. Landlords operating HMOs with five or more tenants from separate households typically require a mandatory licence, while some local authorities impose additional licensing schemes for smaller HMOs. The tribunal found the landlord had committed an offence by operating the property without the required licence throughout the tenancy period.

Landlord's history of non-compliance

The case uncovered a concerning pattern of behaviour, with tribunal documents revealing the landlord had previously faced a separate Rent Repayment Order relating to another unlicensed property. This history likely influenced the tribunal's decision, demonstrating repeated failures to meet licensing obligations.

Councillor Tammy Hymas, Haringey Council's cabinet member for housing, stated: "This case sends a clear message to landlords: if you're breaking the law, we're coming after you. No tenant should have to live in an unlicensed property with mould, serious disrepair and inadequate fire safety measures." The council has pledged to strengthen enforcement against non-compliant landlords through increased inspections and tougher action.

Tenant rights and landlord responsibilities

This case highlights several important considerations for both tenants and landlords:

  • Tenants in HMOs should verify their property holds the appropriate licence through their local council
  • Landlords must ensure properties meet all safety and licensing requirements before letting
  • Rent Repayment Orders can reclaim up to 12 months' rent for unlicensed HMOs
  • Local authorities are increasingly cracking down on non-compliant landlords

Whilst most landlords operate responsibly, cases like this demonstrate the importance of understanding and complying with HMO regulations. Both tenants and landlords may wish to familiarise themselves with local licensing schemes to avoid potential legal and financial consequences.

item.title: Fine & Country and The Guild put rivalry into full swing
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Two leading UK property networks have swapped boardroom meetings for fairway rivalries this week as Fine & Country and The Guild of Property Professionals face off in an unprecedented golf tournament at Celtic Manor. The inaugural Agency Challenge Cup sees 28 players competing across three championship courses in a spirited contest that blends professional camaraderie with competitive fire.

A Three-Day Property Industry Showdown

What began as a modest proposal for a friendly round of golf has evolved into an elaborate three-day tournament complete with team uniforms, live scoring, and even walk-on music for players. The event features fourball better ball matches on The Montgomerie course, singles matches on The Twenty Ten (home of the 2010 Ryder Cup), and concludes with a pairs Texas scramble on Roman Road.

Jonathan Handford, director of Fine & Country Midlands, leads his team with clear ambitions: "We're there to win. The fact we're sister companies makes this even more fun - we know each other well enough to enjoy proper rivalry." Meanwhile, Ian Crampton of Ferndown Estates captains The Guild side with equal determination: "Once we're on the course there will be no favours. We intend to have the bragging rights for the next 12 months."

More Than Just a Golf Tournament

The event represents a novel approach to networking in the property sector, combining professional connections with healthy competition. Iain McKenzie, CEO of The Guild of Property Professionals, highlighted how such events can strengthen industry relationships while allowing participants to "let their hair down" in a competitive setting.

  • 28 professional golfers from both property networks
  • Three championship courses at Celtic Manor
  • Team uniforms and walk-on music creating tournament atmosphere
  • Disciplinary committee overseeing fair play

As the first balls were teed off yesterday, the question remains whether this will become an annual tradition fostering friendly rivalry, or if the competition might prove too intense for sister companies. With a specially commissioned trophy at stake and office WhatsApp groups awaiting the results, both teams appear determined to claim victory - and the year's worth of professional bragging rights that comes with it.

By Bambang Setiawan

As the Renters’ Reform Act continues to reshape the UK rental market, landlords and tenants alike are navigating new challenges and changes. From rising demand for guarantors to delays in repossession cases, the landscape of renting is evolving rapidly. Here’s a closer look at the latest developments affecting the private rental sector.

Rising Demand for Guarantors

Since the introduction of the Renters’ Reform Act, which prohibits landlords from requesting multiple months’ rent in advance, there has been a noticeable increase in tenants being asked to provide a guarantor. According to Housing Hand, a leading tenant referencing company, 37% of renters are unaware of what a guarantor is or how the process works.

Graham Hayward, Managing Director at Housing Hand, highlights that landlords are seeking alternative forms of security. “With tenants no longer able to pay rent upfront, guarantors have become a key requirement for many landlords,” he explains. The company also reports that 37% of renters would be unsure of how to manage if they couldn’t pay their rent, while 33% admit to not planning their finances effectively for the future.

Rent Tribunals Favour Tenants

New analysis by LonRes reveals that rent tribunals are increasingly siding with tenants in disputes over rent increases. The average waiting time for a tribunal hearing is now 96 days nationwide, rising to 142 days in London. Of the 1,325 rent disputes recorded since January 2025, 73% were ruled in favour of tenants, with tribunals finding the proposed rent was too high. Only 18% of cases upheld the landlord’s suggested rent increase.

Chris Welch of LonRes emphasises the importance of landlords setting rent rises accurately and with solid evidence. “Tribunals will never set a higher rent than what the landlord has proposed. They will either lower it or keep it the same. This underscores the need for landlords to ensure their evidence is watertight before initiating a rent increase,” he advises.

Delays in Repossession Cases

The Renters’ Reform Act has also made it more challenging for landlords to regain possession of their properties. A survey by Goodlord found that 25% of landlords now find the process more difficult, with 39% becoming more cautious when vetting potential tenants. Additionally, 9% of landlords are spending more time trying to retain good tenants to avoid the complexities of repossessing a property.

Further research highlights the growing issue of fraudulent tenancy applications, with 41 out of every 1,000 applications flagged as suspicious. These delays and challenges are prompting landlords to rethink their strategies and prioritise thorough tenant checks.

As the rental market adapts to these regulatory changes, both landlords and tenants are encouraged to stay informed and seek professional guidance where necessary. With guarantor requirements, rent tribunals, and repossession delays shaping the sector, understanding these developments is crucial for navigating the evolving landscape of UK renting.

item.title: Record number of landlords taken to court over rent rises – legal experts react
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The number of rental disputes reaching property tribunals has reached unprecedented levels following the implementation of the Renters’ Rights Act. Recent data reveals tribunals made 166 market rent decisions in July alone – nearly four times the figure recorded during the same period last year. With 60% of cases initiated by tenants since the legislation came into force in May, these statistics highlight a dramatic shift in the rental market landscape.

How the Renters’ Rights Act has changed the landscape

The Renters’ Rights Act has fundamentally altered the dynamics between landlords and tenants by abolishing Section 21 'no-fault' evictions. Previously, tenants often hesitated to challenge rent increases due to fears of retaliatory eviction. The removal of this threat, coupled with changes to tribunal processes, appears to have emboldened renters to exercise their rights more freely.

Under the new rules, tenants who unsuccessfully challenge a rent increase only face higher payments from the tribunal decision date, rather than potentially owing backdated amounts. This reduced financial risk has contributed to the surge in cases, with monthly tribunal decisions more than doubling from the pre-legislation average of 42 to 129 in June and 166 in July.

What landlords need to know about rent increases

Legal experts emphasise that landlords must now provide comprehensive evidence to justify proposed rent increases. Simply citing rising costs is no longer sufficient – robust documentation including comparable local lettings, property condition reports, and recent rental transactions is essential.

  • Maintain detailed records of how the proposed rent figure was calculated
  • Follow the statutory Section 13 process precisely
  • Consider property-specific factors like location and amenities
  • Prepare to demonstrate market rent levels with concrete evidence

Property professionals suggest this shift towards evidence-based decision making may lead to more transparent and fairer rental pricing. However, it also places greater administrative responsibilities on landlords to maintain thorough documentation and follow correct procedures.

As the rental market continues to adapt to these legislative changes, both landlords and tenants may benefit from familiarising themselves with the new rules and their implications. With rent challenges becoming more common, understanding the tribunal process and evidence requirements could help prevent disputes before they arise.

item.title: UK property market isn’t broken – but something is definitely blocking it
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK property market continues to show resilience, with buyer demand and housing supply remaining relatively stable. However, recent data suggests that many properties are struggling to progress from listing to completion. According to the latest Property Market Stats for week 33, covering the period ending 23 August, the market is facing challenges that may be slowing transactions. This raises questions about whether current conditions, unrealistic asking prices, or overvaluations are contributing to the issue.

Current Market Trends

In week 33, there were 31,800 new property listings, slightly down from 32,600 the previous week. This figure is below both the 2026 weekly average of 36,300 and the 10-year average for week 33 of 33,000. Year-to-date listings stand at 1.198 million, marginally lower than 2025’s figures but ahead of 2024 and the pre-pandemic 2017–2019 average. Meanwhile, 23,300 homes were sold subject to contract (STC) this week, down from 24,400 the previous week. This figure is also below the 10-year week 33 average of 25,100 and the 2026 weekly average of 24,500. Year-to-date sales STC are 7.2% lower than 2025 and slightly below 2024, though still above pre-pandemic levels.

The Impact of Price Reductions

Price reductions have become a notable feature of the current market, with 23,300 properties seeing price adjustments this week alone. This represents a significant portion of the 767,000 homes currently listed for sale across the UK. The prevalence of reductions suggests that some sellers may be setting initial asking prices too high, leading to longer marketing periods and a higher likelihood of fall-throughs. The data also highlights that the chance of selling decreases the longer a property remains on the market, emphasising the importance of realistic pricing from the outset.

Focus on the Bath Market

The analysis also delves into the Bath property market, comparing local estate agents based on their ability to convert instructions into successful sales rather than focusing solely on market share. This approach provides a more nuanced understanding of agent performance and could help sellers make informed decisions when choosing an agent. The findings underscore the value of selecting an estate agent with a strong track record in achieving completions, particularly in a market where transactions are taking longer to finalise.

While the UK property market remains robust, it is clear that certain factors are hindering the smooth progression of transactions. Homeowners may wish to consider setting realistic asking prices to avoid prolonged marketing periods and potential fall-throughs. Similarly, working with estate agents who have a proven ability to convert listings into sales could be beneficial in navigating the current market conditions.

item.title: Agency boss slams 300% second-home surcharge as housing ‘sticking plaster’
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Edinburgh’s proposed 300% council tax surcharge on second homes has sparked debate about whether the measure will meaningfully address the city’s housing challenges. Local letting agency DJ Alexander has criticised the policy as a "sticking plaster" solution that may fail to deliver promised benefits around affordability and housing supply.

Questionable impact on housing market

Under the council’s plans, owners of second properties and long-term vacant homes could see their council tax bills quadruple. A Band A property would attract an annual charge of £4,336, while Band H homeowners might face £15,935. The council estimates these premiums could generate £4m yearly, while encouraging owners to bring empty properties back into use.

However, critics highlight that Edinburgh’s 1,400 second homes represent just 0.5% of the city’s 265,000-property housing stock. With only 1,700 long-term empty properties, industry experts question whether targeting this small segment will meaningfully affect housing availability or affordability. The limited scale of the policy has led some to suggest its impact may be more symbolic than substantive.

Broader housing challenges persist

Housing campaigners note that Edinburgh faces deeper structural issues. During 2025-26, construction began on just 1,850 new homes - with only 539 being social housing. Meanwhile, the social housing waiting list reached 31,589 applicants last summer, with a third waiting over five years. Homelessness figures reveal 7,866 households (including 3,980 children) were without permanent accommodation in early 2025.

David Alexander of DJ Alexander Scotland commented: "This policy appears to address the housing emergency but is largely performative. The revenue raised is relatively low, it won’t substantially increase affordable homes, and is unlikely to reduce rents or prices as claimed." The agency suggests focusing on accelerating new builds and social housing delivery would prove more effective.

The proposal also raises questions about potential exemptions. Reports suggest MSPs requiring Edinburgh second homes due to distant constituencies may qualify for relief - a detail likely to fuel further debate about fairness and policy effectiveness.

As Edinburgh City Council prepares to vote on the surcharge, the discussion highlights the complex balancing act between generating revenue, discouraging property hoarding, and delivering meaningful solutions to the housing crisis. Homeowners affected by the changes may wish to review their financial planning, whilst housing advocates continue calling for more comprehensive supply-side solutions.
